extracted.intended_audience: institutions receiving Federal financial assistance (higher education and K–12), Title IX coordinators, campus legal counsel, commenters, and other stakeholders in Title IX rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Explanatory preamble responding to public comments on the Department of Education's final Title IX regulations, clarifying statutory interpretation, intersections with the Clery Act, international obligations, procedural requirements, and recipients' obligations (sanctions, remedies, supportive measures, geographic scope, and due process).

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of The Federalist in constitutional interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federalist Papers supply a framework and understanding closely linked to the Constitution's text by some of the authors of that text, but they do not supplant the original public meaning of that text itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use The Federalist as persuasive historical evidence, not as controlling proof of original public meaning when resolving constitutional questions; direct textual and original-public-meaning analysis takes precedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equally Divided Clause and Vice President tie-breaking power
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution permits the Vice President to cast the tie-breaking vote for executive nominations; the Equally Divided Clause preserves the Vice President's authority to break Senate ties for executive and other nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret the Equally Divided Clause as applying to the Vice President's tie-breaking role across Senate floor votes, including confirmation of executive nominees. Arguments denying that role based solely on placement of advice-and-consent in Article II are unpersuasive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpreting Hamilton and The Federalist – majority of voting Senators
rubrics_metrics.description: Hamilton's phrasing in The Federalist indicates that a President needs a majority of the voting Senators (not necessarily a majority of the full Senate) to secure confirmation; abstentions and Senate-determined quorum rules affect who is 'voting.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid conflating 'majority of the full Senate' with 'majority of voting Senators.' Consider Senate rules on quorum and abstentions when assessing confirmation thresholds; historical rhetorical usage may not be precise legal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of clauses across Articles I and II does not negate VP role
rubrics_metrics.description: Placing Senate advice-and-consent powers in Article II while locating the Vice President's tie-breaking language in Article I does not mean the Vice President lacks tie-breaking authority for nominations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for the original constitutional design where President and Vice President could be from different parties; structural placement should be interpreted in historical context rather than assumed to limit functional powers.

rubrics_metrics.name: International treaties and domestic effect (self-executing principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: A treaty (e.g., ICCPR) is not binding domestic law unless Congress has enacted statutes implementing it or the treaty itself conveys an intention that it be 'self-executing' and is ratified on that basis; Senate reservations can render treaty provisions non-self-executing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating alleged conflicts with international law, determine whether the treaty provision is self-executing and whether the Senate entered reservations; if not self-executing (or reserved), domestic statute (e.g., Title IX) governs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of Title IX obligations to ICCPR
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX and the NPRM/final regulations are similar to ICCPR obligations in prohibiting sex discrimination, but where the ICCPR is not self-executing (or subject to reservations), Title IX controls domestic obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess alleged deviations from international norms by comparing textual obligations and by checking treaty reservations and self-execution status; absence of a binding international obligation means domestic statute/regulation determines compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) are non-binding for U.S. law
rubrics_metrics.description: The United States is not legally obligated to abide by the SDGs because the United States never assented to them; they do not occupy the status of customary international law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat SDGs as binding constraints on U.S. regulatory action; consider them aspirational policy goals, not legal limitations, unless and until domestic law adopts them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final regulations protect complainants via supportive measures regardless of investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations require recipients to offer supportive measures designed to restore or preserve the complainant's equal educational access irrespective of whether the recipient also investigates the complaint or whether the respondent is ever found responsible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must provide supportive measures to complainants promptly even if no formal complaint/investigation occurs; supportive measures are distinct from remedies imposed after a finding of responsibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients must provide strong procedural rights in grievance processes
rubrics_metrics.description: When a recipient investigates sexual harassment allegations under Title IX grievance procedures, the final regulations ensure that both complainants and respondents receive strong, clear procedural rights in a fair, truth-seeking grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design grievance procedures that afford transparent investigation and hearing rights to both parties; ensure effective implementation of remedies when responsibility is found.

rubrics_metrics.name: §106.45(b)(1)(vi) — describe range of sanctions or list sanctions
rubrics_metrics.description: A recipient must describe the range of possible sanctions or provide a list of sanctions that the recipient may impose following any determination of responsibility; either a list or a description satisfies §106.45(b)(1)(vi).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions already subject to the Clery Act may satisfy Title IX by listing sanctions as required by Clery; other recipients (e.g., K–12) may describe a range to retain discretion tailored to specific circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies definition and scope after a finding of responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Remedies may include the same individualized services described as 'supportive measures' in §106.30; however, remedies need not be non-disciplinary or non-punitive and need not avoid burdening the respondent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a finding of responsibility, recipients may impose disciplinary or other remedial actions; policies should describe or list possible remedies consistent with §106.45(b)(1)(i) and institutional discretion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive measures discretion and tailoring
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients retain discretion to tailor supportive measures to a party's unique circumstances and may describe a range of supportive measures or list possible measures; they are not limited by the final regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow flexibility to provide individualized supportive measures; policies should indicate available supportive measures while permitting case-specific adaptations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery Act limited scope — applies to institutions receiving Title IV student aid
rubrics_metrics.description: The Clery Act applies only to institutions of higher education that receive Federal student financial aid through Title IV programs; the Clery Act uses the term 'victim' and imposes disclosure and certain notification obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not conflate Clery Act obligations with Title IX obligations for recipients that are not covered postsecondary institutions; if Clery applies, its requirements (e.g., listing sanctions, victim service notices) may satisfy certain Title IX disclosure requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX applies to all recipients of Federal financial assistance
rubrics_metrics.description: These final regulations promulgated under Title IX apply to all recipients of Federal financial assistance (not just Title IV institutions), including elementary and secondary schools that are not subject to the Clery Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame Title IX compliance requirements to fit recipient type and environment; do not impose Clery Act procedures wholesale on recipients never subject to Clery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Department will not respond to comments solely about Clery Act compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Because these final regulations are promulgated under Title IX and not under the Clery Act, the Department will not respond to comments that solely concern compliance with the Clery Act and its implementing regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address Clery-specific compliance through the Clery regulatory framework; comments limited to Clery issues are beyond the scope of Title IX rulemaking and will not be the focus of Title IX responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding perceived conflicts between Clery Act and Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Although certain obligations overlap, institutions subject to both must comply with both sets of regulations; the Department aligned the definition of sexual harassment in §106.30 with the Clery Act to reduce confusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When obligations overlap, ensure institutional policies satisfy both regimes where applicable; aligning definitions can mitigate confusion about duties and covered conduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Due process protections under Title IX aimed at both parties
rubrics_metrics.description: The due process protections required in these final regulations are designed to address sex discrimination specifically for both parties, not just the respondent. A complainant who files a formal complaint benefits from a transparent grievance process under §106.45 that provides both an investigation and a hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design grievance procedures to balance fairness and accuracy for complainants and respondents, with transparent investigative and hearing processes rather than relying solely on Clery Act interpretations of 'prompt, fair, and impartial.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural lawfulness of notice-and-comment rulemaking for Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress does not require negotiated rulemaking to promulgate regulations implementing Title IX; the Department used notice-and-comment rulemaking under the Administrative Procedure Act, which was not arbitrary and capricious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize notice-and-comment (APA) rulemaking as legally appropriate for Title IX regulations; arguments that Title IX requires negotiated rulemaking like Clery are incorrect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geographic limitation for Title IX coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: These final regulations prohibit discrimination on the basis of sex in a recipient's education program or activity against a person in the United States; the only specific geographic limitation respected is Congress's requirement that the discrimination be 'against a person in the United States.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply Title IX obligations only where the victim/complainant is a person in the United States; do not extend Title IX protections extraterritorially beyond that statutory limit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clery geography differences and recipient appropriateness
rubrics_metrics.description: Clery Act requirements and Clery geography were designed for higher education contexts; imposing Clery geography and related reporting on elementary and secondary schools and other recipients would be inappropriate given different populations, environments, and processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor reporting and policy obligations to institutional context; do not force K–12 or non-postsecondary recipients to adopt Clery-style reporting regimes that do not fit their institutional circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to off-campus/online conduct concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations apply to conduct that is part of a recipient's education program or activity against a person in the United States; they do not adopt the broader traditional interpretation that required institutions to respond to harassment regardless of where it occurred worldwide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address off-campus and online incidents to the extent they occur within the recipient's program or activity and affect a person in the United States; recognize statutory geographic limits and ensure policies explain jurisdictional scope.
